newsitem.title: USA: US FCC staff paper says avoid Internet regulation.
newsitem.headline: US FCC staff paper says avoid Internet regulation.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission and other government agencies should try to limit regulation of the Internet computer network, according to an FCC staff working paper issued Thursday.
"Limited government intervention is a major reason why the Internet has grown so rapidly in the United States," said the paper, written by the FCC's Internet expert, Kevin Werbach.
"The federal government's efforts to avoid burdening the Internet with regulation should be looked upon as a major success and should be continued."

Staff working papers represent individual views -- in this case Werbach's -- and do not represent official FCC policy or the policy of any of the agency's commissioners. But the agency so far has been loathe to impose rules on cyberspace.
The paper said the Internet "holds the potential to dramatically change the communications landscape" because it is not tied to traditional models or regulatory environments.
"The Internet creates new forms of competition, valuable services for end users, and benefits to the economy," added the paper, entitled "Digital Tornado: The Internet and Telecommunications Policy."
"Government policy approaches toward the Internet should therefore start from two premises: Avoid unnecessary regulation; and question the applicability of traditional rules," said the paper.
The FCC paper echoes a recent White House draft entitled "Framework for Global Electronic Commerce" which also stresses the need to avoid unnecessary interference with the Internet.

The FCC paper also addresses the issue of increasing the Internet's capacity to handle traffic -- an issue that has spurred some local phone companies to ask the FCC to impose access charges on the global computer network. The agency has signaled it does not plan to do so.
"The FCC should strive to give companies market-efficient incentives to build high-capacity, high-performance networks that are optimized for data transport," said the paper.
"This approach will allow the operation of the market and technological development to resolve difficulties such as congestion and limited bandwidth."
